title: Jekyll and Hyde: Jekyll, Hyde, Utterson and Lanyon
specPoints: Paper 1 Section B: the 19th-century novel, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
AO1: characters; AO2: methods of characterisation

tips.title: Hyde is described by his effect
tips.body: Loathing, the desire to kill, enduring hatred. Nobody can name the deformity.

tips.title: Jekyll was never simply good
tips.body: I concealed my pleasures; a profound duplicity; both sides in dead earnest.

tips.title: Utterson is the method
tips.body: His reserve keeps the secret: Cain's heresy, the envelope locked away.

tips.title: Test pure evil
tips.body: Jekyll says Hyde was pure evil; his own statement says the pleasures were his first.

tips.title: Lanyon dies of knowledge
tips.body: Unscientific balderdash in Chapter 2; shaken to its roots in Chapter 9.

why.matters: The extract question on this novel is almost always about a character or about fear, secrecy or duality through a character. Knowing Hyde by his effect on others, Jekyll by his own confession, Utterson by his reserve and Lanyon by his shock gives an answer something to say about any passage. It also teaches a way of reading people in stories: by what others feel about them, and by testing what they say about themselves.

examples.title: The monster you never quite see
examples.body: Horror films often keep the creature half-seen for as long as they can, because an audience's imagination fills the gap with something worse. Stevenson does it with a face: every character tries to describe Hyde and fails, and the reader supplies the horror.

examples.title: The public figure with a private life
examples.body: News stories about respected people with hidden lives follow the pattern of Jekyll's statement: a public reputation, private pleasures, and a moment when the two meet. The novel asks whether the hidden self was a stranger or the person all along.

steps.title: Hyde: a face nobody can describe
steps.body:
Every character who meets Hyde tries to describe him, and every one fails. That failure is Stevenson's method.

**Enfield** says “He is not easy to describe” (Chapter 1): “something displeasing, something down-right detestable”; “He must be deformed somewhere”. **Utterson** finds him “Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish”; he “gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation”; he has “a sort of murderous mixture of timidity and boldness”; “Something troglodytic, shall we say?” (Chapter 2). The words reach back towards the primitive, a cave-dweller, and the devil: “if ever I read Satan’s signature upon a face, it is on that of your new friend”.

**Their reaction is the description.** Enfield took “I had taken a loathing to my gentleman at first sight”; the doctor at the scene turned “sick and white with the desire to kill him”. Hyde raises “a spirit of enduring hatred” in everyone who sees him. Stevenson describes Hyde by what he does to other people, and leaves the reader to supply the face.

visuals.alt: A table of four attempts by Enfield and Utterson to describe Hyde

check.prompt: Why does Stevenson have every character fail to describe Hyde precisely?
check.solution: Deformity without any nameable malformation: the words point at something and refuse to say what. The June 2024 indicative content noted the imagery of the facelessness of Hyde. An evil that cannot be described is harder to dismiss.

markScheme.description: So the fear comes from what cannot be named, and each reader supplies their own image of evil

options: So the fear comes from what cannot be named, and each reader supplies their own image of evil
Because Hyde wears a mask throughout the novel
Because nobody ever sees Hyde
Because Stevenson had not decided what Hyde looked like when he began the novel, and wanted the illustrator of the first edition to design Hyde's appearance for the readers

steps.title: Hyde in action: calm, then fury
steps.body:
**Calm cruelty.** In Chapter 1 he “trampled calmly over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground”; “it was like some damned Juggernaut”. The horror is the calm.

**Fury.** In Chapter 4, “with ape-like fury”, he beats an old man to death so that “the bones were audibly shattered”. The animal images, the ape and the troglodyte, suggest something from before civilisation.

**Inside Hyde.** In Chapter 10 Jekyll describes being Hyde: “I felt younger, lighter, happier in body” (Chapter 10). After the murder, “With a transport of glee, I mauled the unresisting body” (Chapter 10). In the last pages, “his love of life is wonderful” (Chapter 10): even Jekyll, who fears him, pities Hyde's clinging to life. Jekyll calls him “Edward Hyde, alone in the ranks of mankind, was pure evil”, and yet this Hyde is afraid.

**Smaller than Jekyll.** Hyde is “so much smaller, slighter and younger than Henry Jekyll”, because, Jekyll thinks, the evil side of him had been less exercised. The body is the history of a character.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of Hyde's course: tramples a child calmly, beats Carew with ape-like fury, is hunted and hides, and dies by his own hand

check.prompt: Why is Hyde smaller than Jekyll, according to Jekyll's statement?
check.solution: Jekyll suggests the evil side of his nature, less exercised and less exhausted than the good, was less robust and less developed. The body is a moral record: the self that had been repressed is smaller and younger.

markScheme.description: The evil side of his nature had been less exercised than the good, so it had grown less

options: Because Jekyll is very tall
The evil side of his nature had been less exercised than the good, so it had grown less
Because the potion was too strong and shrank Jekyll's body every time he drank it, which is why he needed a larger dose each time and why Hyde grew smaller in each chapter of the novel
Because Hyde is a child

steps.title: Jekyll: respectable, and never simply good
steps.body:
**The public man.** Jekyll is “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty” (Chapter 3), with every mark of capacity and kindness, a doctor with degrees after his name, rich and generous. His friends dine at his house.

**The private man.** In Chapter 10 he admits that even before the drug “I concealed my pleasures” (Chapter 10) and lived “a profound duplicity of life”. He is careful to say “I was in no sense a hypocrite” (Chapter 10): “both sides of me were in dead earnest”.

**What the drug gave him.** Not a new evil but freedom: “I was the first that could plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability” (Chapter 10) and then “spring headlong into the sea of liberty”. He took pleasure in it, until “I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self”.

**His end.** He calls himself “I am the chief of sinners, I am the chief of sufferers also” (Chapter 6), and signs off “I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end”. Jekyll wanted the pleasures of Hyde without the consequences for Jekyll; the novel shows that there is no such bargain.

visuals.alt: A table of Jekyll's public and private lives, with a line for each

check.prompt: What does Jekyll mean when he says he was in no sense a hypocrite, and both sides of him were in dead earnest?
check.solution: He claims that the man who laboured for knowledge and the man who plunged in shame were both himself. The claim matters for interpretation: Hyde is not a stranger but a part of Jekyll set free.

markScheme.description: Both his respectable and his hidden selves were genuinely him, not a mask over a truth

options: That he was a completely good man whose only mistake was the experiment, and that Hyde was a separate being who entered his body from outside when he drank the potion in his laboratory
That he never told a lie in his life
Both his respectable and his hidden selves were genuinely him, not a mask over a truth
That he did not enjoy being Hyde

steps.title: Utterson: the loyal lawyer
steps.body:
**Reserved and tolerant.** Utterson is “a man of a rugged countenance that was never lighted by a smile”, lean and dusty, “and yet somehow lovable” (Chapter 1). He says “I incline to Cain’s heresy” (Chapter 1), and he is often “the last good influence in the lives of downgoing men” (Chapter 1).

**The investigator.** He reads the will, watches the door, “I shall be Mr. Seek”, meets Hyde, questions Jekyll. He sees clues and misreads them, as in “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer”.

**The protector of reputation.** He wants to know and does not want to know. He locks away Lanyon's envelope unopened; he does not share his suspicions; when he enters the cabinet his first thought is for his friend's good name.

**Why he matters.** He is the reader's guide, and his reserve is the novel's method: a respectable man who will not ask the question that would ruin a friend. The mystery lasts as long as it does because Utterson is the kind of man he is.

boxes.title: Tolerant
boxes.body: Cain's heresy: let a man go his own way

boxes.title: Investigator
boxes.body: If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek

visuals.alt: Four boxes on Utterson: reserved, tolerant, the investigator, and the protector of reputation

check.prompt: How does Utterson's character help to keep the mystery going?
check.solution: Utterson is the last good influence for men in trouble, and he does not judge. The same tolerance makes him keep secrets, lock away Lanyon's envelope and hesitate to act. His character is part of the structure.

markScheme.description: His loyalty and reserve mean he protects Jekyll's reputation and will not ask the question that would expose him

options: Because he is away from London for most of the novel
Because he is a poor lawyer who does not understand wills or letters, and he misses every clue in the novel until Poole explains the whole mystery to him in the cabinet in Chapter 8
Because he is secretly working with Hyde

steps.title: Lanyon: the scientist who cannot bear it
steps.body: Lanyon is Jekyll's old friend and fellow doctor, and his story is a short tragedy of its own.

visuals.problem: What does Lanyon's story add to the novel?

steps.text: In Chapter 2 he is “a hearty, healthy, dapper, red-faced gentleman”. He has fallen out with Jekyll over his science: “unscientific balderdash”.
steps.note: The rational man of conventional science, healthy and certain.

steps.text: At the transformation in Chapter 9 he is taunted as a man “you who have denied the virtue of transcendental medicine”.
steps.note: His disbelief in what Jekyll calls transcendental science is exactly what is tested.

steps.text: He sees the change: “there stood Henry Jekyll”.
steps.note: The impossible, witnessed by the one man most sure it was impossible.

steps.text: The result: “My life is shaken to its roots” (Chapter 9); “I have had a shock”; within weeks he is dead.
steps.note: Knowledge that his world cannot hold kills him.

steps.text: He leaves the truth in a sealed enclosure, marked not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Jekyll.
steps.note: Even the scientist keeps the secret: he writes it down and will not speak it.

visuals.alt: A table comparing Lanyon and Jekyll: their science, how each first appears, and how each ends

check.prompt: Why does seeing the transformation kill Lanyon?
check.solution: My life is shaken to its roots. Lanyon had dismissed Jekyll's science as unscientific balderdash; to see Hyde become Jekyll proves him wrong in a way he cannot survive. His death shows what the knowledge costs a respectable mind.

markScheme.description: It destroys the rational, material view of the world his life rested on

options: It destroys the rational, material view of the world his life rested on
Because Hyde poisons him with the draught after the transformation, to stop him telling the police what he has seen, and Lanyon dies of the poison two weeks later in his house in Cavendish Square
Because he is very old
Because Utterson tells him bad news

steps.title: The others: Enfield, Poole, Guest, Carew
steps.body:
**Enfield,** Utterson's distant kinsman, tells the first story and ends the chapter by agreeing never to refer to it again: a gentleman's discretion. He is with Utterson at the window in Chapter 7.

**Poole,** Jekyll's butler, has served him for twenty years. He brings Utterson to the cabinet in Chapter 8 and is the first to say what the voice is not: “that thing was not my master”.

**Mr Guest,** Utterson's head clerk and a student of handwriting, sees the truth in two letters: “the two hands are in many points identical: only differently sloped”.

**Sir Danvers Carew,** “an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair”, is Hyde's victim: a kindly, elderly Member of Parliament. His goodness makes the murder worse, and his rank makes it a public scandal.

rows: Tells the first story; agrees to silence
Knows the voice is not his master's
Sees the same hand, differently sloped

steps.title: Plan an answer on Hyde and fear
steps.body:
Take the June 2024 question: *Starting with this extract, explore how Stevenson creates an atmosphere of fear and danger.* The extract was Utterson alone at night thinking about Hyde. Plan the character part of it in five lines.

1. The idea: the fear comes from what cannot be seen or named.
2. In the extract: the faceless figure, the child crushed at every corner.
3. Hyde described elsewhere: deformity without any nameable malformation.
4. Hyde in action: the Carew murder.
5. The effect on others: loathing, the desire to kill, Lanyon's shock.

Then write the paragraph on the effect on others.

boxes.body: Fear of what cannot be named

check.solution: The Sawbones, a doctor of no great feeling, wants to kill Hyde on sight. The June 2024 indicative content lists the effect of Hyde on other characters. Fear that makes respectable people feel violence is a danger that spreads.

markScheme.description: Even a calm doctor turns sick and white with the desire to kill him: Hyde makes others violent

options: Everybody in the novel likes Hyde at first and only becomes afraid of him after the Carew murder, when the newspapers report that he is wanted by the police for the killing of a Member of Parliament

Hyde makes the other characters laugh

steps.title: Interpretations: is Hyde evil, or is Jekyll?
steps.body:
Jekyll's own theory is that “commingled out of good and evil”, and that Hyde, “Edward Hyde, alone in the ranks of mankind, was pure evil”, is the evil part separated out. A top-level answer tests that theory rather than repeating it.

**For the theory.** Hyde's acts are cruel without motive; everyone who sees him feels revulsion; he is smaller, as if less developed.

**Against it.** Jekyll had “I concealed my pleasures” long before Hyde; he chose to drink again; he enjoyed the freedom; and he says both sides were him. Hyde looks less like a separate evil and more like Jekyll's permission to himself.

**The reading that holds both.** Stevenson presents Hyde as the part of a respectable man that respectability forbids, and the danger is less that he exists than that Jekyll wanted him.

boxes.title: So
boxes.body: Hyde is permission, not a stranger

visuals.alt: Four boxes testing Jekyll's claim that Hyde is pure evil: the case for, and three points against

check.prompt: Which sentence explores Jekyll's claim that Hyde was pure evil in the way the top level rewards?
check.solution: The top level asks for interpretations explored. Weighing Jekyll's claim against his own admissions does that. Accepting the claim because Jekyll is respectable is the very trust the novel undermines.

markScheme.description: Jekyll calls Hyde pure evil, but he had concealed his pleasures long before and chose to drink again, so Hyde is his permission

options: Hyde is evil because he kills Carew

Jekyll calls Hyde pure evil, but he had concealed his pleasures long before and chose to drink again, so Hyde is his permission

steps.title: The characters in one page
steps.body:
A face nobody can describe; a respectable man who wanted a holiday from himself; a lawyer who protects his friend; a scientist killed by what he saw.

- **Hyde:** pale and dwarfish; deformity without any nameable malformation; troglodytic; Juggernaut; ape-like fury; smaller than Jekyll; loves life.
- **Jekyll:** smooth-faced, capacity and kindness; concealed pleasures; a profound duplicity; both sides in dead earnest; the chief of sinners.
- **Utterson:** rugged, reserved, tolerant, lovable; Mr Seek; protector of reputation.
- **Lanyon:** hearty and certain; unscientific balderdash; shaken to its roots; dies.
- **The others:** Enfield's silence, Poole's twenty years, Guest's eye, Carew's innocence.
- **Interpretation:** is Hyde pure evil, or Jekyll's permission to himself?

questions.solution: Lanyon says Jekyll began to go wrong, wrong in mind, and calls his science unscientific balderdash. The disagreement is about what science may do, and Chapter 9 settles it.

questions.solution: Plod and load make respectability heavy; spring headlong and the sea make freedom light. The contrast in the verbs is the temptation: both lives, and no cost to the first.

questions.solution: Cain asked whether he was his brother's keeper. Utterson borrows the phrase for his own tolerance. It makes him a good friend to men in trouble, and a slow investigator.

questions.prompt: Why might Stevenson make Carew an aged and beautiful gentleman and a Member of Parliament?
questions.solution: The maid sees him bow with old-world kindness before Hyde strikes. A gentle old man and a public figure: the victim chosen so that the crime is as shocking and as public as possible.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Stevenson presents Hyde through other characters' reactions to him.
questions.solution: Stevenson presents Hyde less by describing him than by describing what he does to the people who see him. Enfield cannot explain it: “He is not easy to describe”, only “something displeasing, something down-right detestable”, and he admits “I had taken a loathing to my gentleman at first sight”. The doctor called to the child, a man of no strong feeling, turned “sick and white with the desire to kill him”. Utterson, the most tolerant man in the novel, reaches for the devil: “if ever I read Satan’s signature upon a face, it is on that of your new friend”. Each reaction is stronger than the evidence explains, because Hyde “gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation”, and the reader is left with the response and no cause. The method makes the fear grow in the gap. It also reveals the respectable men: the calm doctor who wants to kill, the gentleman who takes a loathing at first sight. Hyde calls up in them the violence they would never admit, which is exactly what he is in Jekyll.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Stevenson presents Jekyll as responsible for Hyde.
questions.solution: Jekyll's statement argues that “man is not truly one, but truly two” and that Hyde was “Edward Hyde, alone in the ranks of mankind, was pure evil”, but its own evidence makes Jekyll responsible. Before any drug he “I concealed my pleasures” and lived “a profound duplicity of life”; the experiment did not create a wish but satisfied one. He describes the freedom with relish, able to “I was the first that could plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability” and then “spring headlong into the sea of liberty”, and he chose to drink again. He even denies being a hypocrite, because “both sides of me were in dead earnest”. By his own account, then, Hyde is Jekyll with the restraints removed. Stevenson places this confession at the very end, so that the reader, who has spent eight chapters seeing a respectable doctor through the eyes of his loyal friends, discovers that respectability was the problem: it made Jekyll hide what he wanted, and the drug let him have it without paying.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "Utterson is boring and does nothing." What is the better account?
questions.solution: Utterson is the narrative's focus for eight chapters, and his character shapes what the reader learns. His tolerance, discretion and protection of reputation are the novel's subject as well as its method.

questions.prompt: What does Lanyon represent, set beside Jekyll?
questions.solution: Lanyon is the hearty, healthy doctor of material science who calls Jekyll's work balderdash. He is taunted for having denied transcendental medicine, and the proof destroys him. He stands for the limits the Victorian scientific mind set itself.

markScheme.description: Conventional, material science, certain of its limits until the transformation proves them wrong

options: The criminal underworld of Soho, which Jekyll visits as Hyde and which Lanyon secretly controls, which is why he refuses to see Jekyll after the Carew murder in the sixth chapter
The church
The police
Conventional, material science, certain of its limits until the transformation proves them wrong

examTechnique.body:
**Hyde by effect.** Quote the reactions: loathing, the desire to kill, enduring hatred. Name the method: fear of what cannot be described.

**Jekyll by confession.** Use Chapter 10, and test it.

**Utterson as method.** His reserve is why the mystery lasts.

**Lanyon as science.** His death measures what the knowledge costs.
examinerErrors: Describing Hyde as simply ugly, when the text says his deformity cannot be named.
Treating Jekyll as good and Hyde as a separate villain.
Leaving Utterson out, when the narrative follows him for eight chapters.
Quoting loosely: learn the exact words of the key descriptions.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer reads the characters as methods. It shows Hyde through the reactions he provokes, reads Jekyll's statement critically and tests his claim that Hyde was pure evil, and treats Utterson's reserve and Lanyon's shock as the novel's way of showing respectable men meeting what they will not name. Quotations are exact and chosen from across the novel.
